name: John von Neumann
role: Hungarian-American mathematician and physicist; member of the US Atomic Energy Commission 1955-57 (1903-1957)
summary: Von Neumann, mathematician and architect of game theory and the stored-program computer, advised the US military on nuclear weapons and missiles and sat on the Atomic Energy Commission. His published political views are few: a 1955 Fortune essay warning that technology outruns the planet and that only a long sequence of small, correct decisions can help.

gradual-change.rationale: Wrote in 1955: 'What safeguard remains? Apparently only day-to-day, or perhaps year-to-year, opportunistic measures, a long sequence of small, correct decisions', and 'we can specify only the human qualities required: patience, flexibility, intelligence'.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: Wrote in 1955 that 'the crisis does not arise from accidental events or human errors. It is inherent in technology's relation to geography on the one hand and to political organization on the other', that technology is useful and constructive but 'also dangerous', and that the remaining safeguard is not a cure but human qualities.

notes: Von Neumann left almost no political writing. The 1955 Fortune essay, read in an English scan from his Collected Works (Internet Archive ETC3234), gives two answers: tech-solves-problems -1 medium and gradual-change +1 medium. The widely quoted remark 'If you say why not bomb them tomorrow, I say why not today?' (LIFE, 25 February 1957, about 1950) is not used: the issue could not be read (see notFound) and a 1992 review's report of it is not an original. Not answered: military-superiority and deterrence (his Teapot Committee and Atomic Energy Commission roles are acts known to me only from Wikipedia), defeat-communism (no stated general priority), the weather-control passage (a forecast of a risk). Failing the uncertainty rule is the expected outcome.
